messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Carpenter
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 61

He is a 30-year-old married carpenter who comes to therapy after months of feeling as if part of him is still standing in the middle of a jobsite, unable to move. The event that changed things happens on a construction project he is helping frame with a small crew. It is a routine workday until, in an instant, a coworker falls from a scaffold. He sees the body hit the ground, hears the sound, and then watches the scene turn chaotic around him. Someone is shouting for help. Another man is already on the phone with emergency services. He feels frozen, aware of the smell of dust and cut lumber, aware of his own hands shaking, but unable to make himself step forward in the way he thinks he should. In the weeks after, that moment replays with a stubborn clarity, as if his mind keeps returning him to the exact place where he stood.

At first, he tells himself he is just shaken up and that time will settle it. He goes back to work, because that is what he knows how to do. Carpentry has always been a steadying thing for him: measuring twice, cutting clean lines, making sense of wood and hardware and plans. But after the accident, the worksite no longer feels neutral. Heights catch his attention immediately. Scaffolds, ladders, even the edge of a roof can make his stomach tighten. He notices himself scanning for hazards before he can focus on the task in front of him. He becomes more tense around tools and moving equipment, more irritable when coworkers move too quickly or joke about safety. He begins taking extra time with simple jobs, not because he is careless, but because he cannot shake the sense that something bad is always about to happen.

At home, his wife notices that he is present in body but often somewhere else in his head. He sits through dinner with his phone face down beside him, listening to her talk, but he misses parts of what she says because he is caught in his own replay of the accident. At night, when he finally lies down, sleep does not come easily. He drifts off exhausted, then wakes abruptly from dreams he cannot always remember in detail, but from which he rises sweating and tense, his heart pounding. Sometimes he sits on the edge of the bed for several minutes before going back to sleep, staring into the dark and trying to convince himself that he is in his own house and not back on the jobsite. His wife asks what is wrong, and he says he is fine more often than he means to.

He tries not to talk about the accident because each time he starts, he feels the pressure building behind his eyes and in his chest. He does not want to be the kind of man who falls apart over something he witnessed rather than something that happened directly to him. That belief leaves him ashamed, which makes him withdraw further. He stops going for beers with coworkers after work, partly because he does not want to hear the story retold and partly because being around them brings the memory too close. He keeps busy with projects around the house, but even there he finds himself suddenly back in the scene, hit by a wave of nausea or a sharp jolt of fear when he hears a loud noise nearby. A dropped hammer, a truck backfiring, the sudden scrape of metal on concrete can pull him into the memory before he has time to prepare.

He notices changes in himself that feel harder to name than fear. He is more on edge, quicker to snap, and then feels guilty afterward. He has less patience with noise, clutter, interruptions. He is tired in a way that rest does not fix. When he is driving, he sometimes becomes aware that he is gripping the wheel too hard, as though bracing for impact. He catches himself thinking about what he could have done differently that day, running through useless scenarios in which he is faster, closer, more decisive. Those thoughts do not bring relief; they only leave him more stuck in the feeling that he failed to respond correctly.

By the time he arrives in therapy, months have passed and the accident still sits close to the surface of everything he does. He speaks about his work with the kind of precision he uses on a framing square, but his voice tightens when the scaffold is mentioned. He says he is still working, still married, still functioning, but it takes constant effort to hold himself together. Underneath that effort is a man who keeps bracing for the next fall, the next loud impact, the next moment when he will again be powerless to stop what he sees.
